newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain truck strike gravely damages economy-cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Spain truck strike gravely damages economy-cabinet.

text.p: Spain's government said Friday that a nine-day-old truckers' strike was inflicting "grave damage" on the economy.
"This is a savage and unjustified strike which is causing grave damage to the national economy," Development Minister Rafael Arias Salgado said after a weekly cabinet meeting.

Salgado said the strike was led by a "violent and radical minority." Earlier the minister had intimated the strike was being manipulated from behind the scenes for reasons unrelated to the strikers' demands.
He pledged that the government would assure unimpeded travel on its roads.
The strike, to press demands for better working conditions and lower fuel prices, began in northern Spain but by Friday was burgeoning into a full-blown economic crisis.
The agriculture sector has lost some 20 billion pesetas ($140.3 million) so far with milk, meat and vegetables worst hit, a farmer's cooperative estimated.
The Economy Ministry warned a continuation of the strike would cause a steep increase in fish and produce prices.
The strike looked set to broaden, with taxi unions calling on members to join the strike Monday.
Strikers have choked roads in the north, cut off supplies to many areas and forced factories to shut.
By Friday, the chaos was spreading south.
In a reprise of the truckers' strike in France last year that disrupted much of Western Europe with a 12-day blockade, Spanish drivers are demanding a revamp of the industry.
They want the retirement age lowered to 60 years from 65 and are pushing for curbs on surging fuel prices, a revision of tariffs and recognition of professional illnesses.

The cabinet Friday introduced deregulatory measures aimed at lowering the cost of fuel distribution, a step which a leading union welcomed. But the union made clear it would not call off the strike after the decision.

"The measure is one we requested but we're also asking for other things and aside from that we'd like to have professional fuel prices, with a subsidy, such as other sectors like farming and fisheries," spokesman Jose Manuel Martinez said.

The government criticised the union for boycotting negotiations to end the strike. Representatives from the development, labour, economy and industry ministries met a number of transport associations Thursday but the lead union, Fedatrans, refused to go.

"An end to the strike will only be achieved if the cabinet calls an urgent meeting to create an interministerial commission with powers to coordinate restructuring of the sector," Fedatrans said in a statement.
Meanwhile, truckers tightened their grip on Spain's roads and blocked ports as the strike spread.
Thousands of trucks lined the shoulders of main roads and pickets initimidated any drivers who dared to pass.
With truckers blockading border crossings, hundreds of foreign drivers also found themselves caught up in the jam.
More than a thousand Portuguese trucks were stranded at the border at Vilar Formoso and Caia, and hundreds of French trucks were also stuck at Behovia-Irun, local media said.
